schools.summary: Henry reads the timing as calculated malice — the near-finished wall makes it now or never, so the enemies turn from open attack to wheedling Nehemiah into a village of Benjamin under fair pretexts, while he, forewarned, trusts them not.

Keil and Delitzsch fix the passive idiom and the parenthesis on the unhung doors; Ellicott notes 'the Three' always have pre-eminence and reads the door-clause as a note of historical accuracy pointing back to the anticipation of Neh. 3.
Gill marks simply that the wall was now quite finished, the breaches all made up.

themes: the wall finished but the doors unhung
enemies turning from force to fraud
the lure to a village of Benjamin

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch give the proposal and its menacing aside; Ellicott reads Tobiah's demotion to 'secretary' and fixes the meeting at Hakkephirim in the plain of Ono, over twenty miles off — the distance itself the trap.

Clarke names the purpose — to lure Nehemiah from his friends and carry him off or murder him at Ono in Benjamin; Wesley supplies the fair pretext of consulting the king's service or a friendly accommodation.
Gill notes the summons came formally, by messengers.

themes: the lure to the plain of Ono
a courteous invitation, a deadly purpose
drawing the shepherd from the flock

schools.summary: Clarke reads the prudence of not naming the plot (lest the enemies go to extremities) and makes 'I am doing a great work' the model answer of every laborer beset by trifling or malicious interruptions.
Henry calls the reply heaven-taught: Nehemiah's one care that the work not cease, giving a true reason without reproaching their treachery — 'compliment must always give way to business.'
Gill notes the measured manner — no open contempt, and answer sent by his own people rather than by their messenger.

themes: prudence in not naming the plot

schools.summary: Henry sees the repeated refusal as vexatious to plotters who aimed at the ceasing of the work, and draws the rule that repeated urgency must be met with the same reason and resolution.
Wesley makes the constancy a principle — never overcome by importunity to do anything ill or imprudent.
Keil and Delitzsch note the fixed phrasing (comp. 2 Sam. 15:6) and the identical answer each time.
Gill marks the enemies' pressing eagerness to get Nehemiah into their hands.

themes: the aim was the ceasing of the work

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark the shift to an open letter and its charge; Ellicott recalls the four ironic refusals and reads the unsealed silken bag as a move from enticement to intimidation, meant to alarm Nehemiah that the slander was already public.
Clarke reads the unsealed letter as a studied insult to a governor (Eastern letters being folded, bagged, and sealed); Wesley takes its openness as parading the charge as common talk.
Gill notes Sanballat now wrote alone, without Tobiah or Geshem, feigning a warmer friendship.

themes: a slander made to seem public

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch lay out the whole charge — rebellion, kingship, hired prophets, the threat of report to the king — aimed at forcing a self-clearing interview; Ellicott savours Nehemiah's exact quotation ('Gashmu'), the appeal to the heathen and the Persian court, and prophecy twisted into ambition.
Gill hears in 'reported among the heathen' the pretence of a wide public rumour noised abroad in every mouth.

themes: a charge of rebellion and kingship
the Persian king invoked as threat

schools.summary: Gill exposes the projection — Sanballat and Tobiah, who had themselves been hiring prophets against Nehemiah, now charge him with appointing prophets to proclaim him king.

Clarke reads 'let us take counsel' as 'come and justify yourself,' a trick to get Nehemiah into Sanballat's power; Wesley glosses 'a king in Judah' as pretended revolt and the counsel as a feigned offer to clear his innocence.

themes: prophets alleged to proclaim a king
'come and clear yourself' as a snare

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch weigh the verb 'feignest' — from a root meaning to invent or fabricate, as at 1 Kings 12:33 — so the charge is not error but deliberate invention out of Sanballat's own heart.
Clarke admires the composure: 'you well know what you say is false; I shall not trouble myself about a false charge.'
Gill notes the reply was sent, whether by letter or messenger the text leaves unsaid.

themes: a flat denial of the slander
the calm of a clear conscience

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch fix the enemies' aim (to weaken the workers' hands) and explain the abrupt imperative 'strengthen my hands' as the writer reliving his prayer; Ellicott reads it as an interjectional petition, the words 'O God' being a supplied insertion.
Henry makes it a theology of dependence — grace fetched by prayer to strengthen the hands the enemy would weaken — and notes some read it as a resolution, 'I will strengthen my hands.'
Wesley commends it as a pattern prayer for entering any service or conflict.
Gill takes 'they all made us afraid' of Sanballat's circle or of all the surrounding heathen, whose scandal aimed to intimidate.

themes: the aim to weaken the builders' hands

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott expose Shemaiah as a hired false prophet, feigning seclusion and a nocturnal threat, urging Nehemiah to flee into the holy place and bar the doors — a lure into an illegal act that would give occasion to defame him.

Clarke shows the counsel would have left the people leaderless and Nehemiah's government seemingly ended, with Sanballat seizing power; Wesley reads the 'shut up' as a pretence of singular devotion and Spirit-given knowledge of danger.

Henry names the strategy — to drive the cautious governor into hiding, anywhere but at his work — and calls it the devil's work, temptation wearing the dress of revelation, brought by prophet and prophetess.
Gill takes Shemaiah for a priest of the course of Delaiah whom Nehemiah esteemed and came to consult.

themes: the lure to flee into the temple
temptation in the dress of devotion
driving the leader from his work

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note the ambiguity of 'to save his life' — or, under Numbers 18:7, to forfeit it — and Ellicott divides the verse into personal dignity and a layman's scruple against entering the holy place, reading 'and live?'
Clarke and Wesley press the argument from office — the governor, appointed by God and king, may not desert the flock; to flee would dishonour God and betray the people.
Gill notes that Nehemiah's flight would have scattered the people and left the wall defenceless — the plotters' aim.

themes: 'should such a man as I flee?'
a layman forbidden the holy place
the shepherd may not desert the flock

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note Nehemiah perceived it from Shemaiah's conduct once his advice was refused, and that the Hebrew emphatically denies God sent him — Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him.
Henry makes it a lesson in discernment: the advice betrayed a design against Nehemiah, and the wickedness of such mercenary men will be brought to light.
Gill gives the test — God had not sent him, because his counsel ran against the cause of God and true religion.

Keil and Delitzsch unfold the strung purpose-clauses — fear leading to sinful flight into the holy place, a desecration that would furnish matter for an evil report; Ellicott sums it as a plot to discredit the governor as a violator of the law.
Henry gathers the two dreads — offending God and shaming himself; next to the sinfulness of sin we should dread its scandalousness.
Wesley spells out the double snare — to enter a forbidden place both sinfully and shamefully, and so be branded a guilty coward before his people and the Persian king.
Gill marks the plain design — hired that Nehemiah should be afraid and act on the fear.

themes: hired to make him fear and sin
a trespass made into an evil report
dreading sin and its scandal alike

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch gather Noadiah and the rest of the fear-mongering prophets under the petition; Ellicott frames it as an official prophetic prayer committing God's cause to God, and finds Noadiah's obscurity an indirect proof of the record's truth.
Henry guards the prayer from vengefulness — as with 'think upon me, my God' (Neh. 5:19), Nehemiah imprecates no particular judgment but refers the cause to the righteous Judge.
Gill reads it as a plea that God both disappoint and duly reward the plotters' works.
Clarke doubts the feminine 'prophetess,' judging the ending a scribal error for 'Noadiah the prophet,' as the versions read.

debates.question: Was Noadiah a prophetess, or should the text read 'Noadiah the prophet'?

sides.position: A prophetess, as the Hebrew stands — a real woman among the hired false prophets
The feminine ending is a scribal error; read 'Noadiah the prophet,' with the ancient versions

themes: the cause committed to God, not avenged

schools.summary: Henry marvels at fifty-two days (with sabbath rests) — threats that quickened rather than weakened, 'out of the eater came forth meat' (Judg. 14:14), and much work done in earnest.

Ellicott dates the 25th of Elul to about 15 September, defends the short span given ready materials and organized bands (no need of Josephus's two years four months), and hears in 'wrought of our God' divine help, not miracle, with Nehemiah's own part forgotten.
Clarke defends the fifty-two days — old wall and foundations largely standing, materials at hand — citing Caesar, Titus, and Alexander; Wesley dates Elul to August–September.
Gill fixes the twenty-fifth of Elul, the sixth month, to August–September.

themes: the wall finished in fifty-two days

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch explain the unique idiom 'cast down in their own eyes' by the fallen countenance of Gen. 4:5 and the failing courage of 1 Sam. 17:32; Ellicott sums it — the enemies heard, saw, and were ashamed.
Henry unfolds their shame, envy, and despair, marvelling that even heathen owned a special providence — 'the Lord hath done great things for them' (Ps. 126:2).
Clarke reads 'wrought of our God' as an especial providence so plain that carnal enemies could discern it.
Gill notes the enemies heard the wall was finished.

themes: the enemies cast down in their own eyes

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read it as Nehemiah's supplementary note — the nobles multiplying letters to and from Tobiah because of his marriage into a Jewish family; Ellicott confirms the large, steady correspondence.
Clarke marks the peril — enemies without and false friends within — judging that any lesser man than Nehemiah would have failed to re-establish Jerusalem.
Henry feels the disgrace that nobles of Judah should keep familiar correspondence with an enemy — great men not always wise or honest.
Gill sets the correspondence 'in those days,' while the wall was building.

Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott map the two marriage-ties — Tobiah son-in-law of Shecaniah ben Arah (Ezra 2:5), his son wed to a daughter of the builder Meshullam (Neh. 3:4), even Eliashib related (Neh. 13:4) — the affinity ripening into a sworn conspiracy; the Hebrew names suggest naturalised Ammonites of Hebrew extraction.
Clarke sets it in the wider plague of mixed marriage (Neh. 13:23; Ezra 9:3), the nobles so imbued with idolatry that they forgot God, brethren, and their own souls.
Henry's maxim — once akin to Tobiah, soon sworn to him; a sinful love leads to a sinful league.
Gill notes many were bound to Tobiah by an oath to serve his interest and follow his advice.

outliers.note: Argues Tobiah and his son, though naturalised Ammonites, were really of Hebrew extraction — which eased the intermarriage — where Clarke stresses rather their heathen, idolatrous character.

themes: a sinful love, a sinful league

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch expose the two-way traffic — Tobiah's good qualities praised to Nehemiah, Nehemiah's words carried back to Tobiah — which, without distortion, still played into his hands and fed his frightening letters; Ellicott reads it as an intelligence system enabling the disquieting letters.

Henry marks the impudence of courting Nehemiah into friendship with a bad man ('those that forsake the law praise the wicked,' Prov. 28:4) and betraying his counsels, closing on 'God thought upon him for good.'
Gill notes the nobles reported Tobiah's good deeds, recommending him as worthy of Nehemiah's friendship.

themes: praising the wicked, betraying the good
their thoughts for evil, God's for good
